{"user":"I’m writing a literature review for my thesis on how social media use affects adolescent mental health. Can you outline a solid structure (section headings) and suggest what kinds of studies and variables I should include?","plus_response":"Absolutely. Here’s a solid literature-review structure you can use, plus the study types and variables that typically make the review more coherent and easier to defend academically:

1) Introduction
- Brief framing of the adolescent population and the relevance of social media
- Scope and key research question(s)
- Definitions (e.g., “social media use,” “mental health,” “adolescents”) and inclusion criteria

2) Conceptual Framework and Key Constructs
- Theoretical lenses (e.g., displacement, social comparison, uses & gratification)
- Definitions of exposures: type of use (active vs passive), platform characteristics, intensity/frequency, duration
- Definitions of outcomes: depressive symptoms, anxiety symptoms, loneliness, self-esteem, wellbeing, stress

3) Overview of the Empirical Literature
- Organization by study design (cross-sectional vs longitudinal vs experimental/natural experiments)
- Organization by mechanism (e.g., social comparison, cyberbullying exposure, sleep disruption)
- Brief synthesis of what each design can/can’t establish

4) Findings by Exposure Type
- Active engagement vs passive consumption
- Platform features (e.g., algorithmic feeds, messaging) where studies distinguish them
- Contextual moderators commonly studied

5) Variables, Measurement Choices, and Operationalization Issues
- Common scales for mental health outcomes
- How social media use is measured (self-report vs behavioral data)
- Measurement validity, common-method bias, and confounding control

6) Moderators and Mediators
- Moderators: baseline mental health, age, gender, socioeconomic status, offline relationships, personality traits, parenting/family factors
- Mediators: sleep quality, perceived social support, body image concerns, stress appraisal, loneliness

7) Causality, Reverse Causation, and Confounding
- How studies handle selection effects (propensity approaches, fixed effects, cross-lagged models)
- Reverse causation evidence and robustness checks

8) Methodological Limitations and Research Gaps
- Heterogeneity in definitions and measurement
- Attrition/bias in longitudinal work
- Geographic, cultural, and sample differences

9) Synthesis and Emerging Directions
- A concise narrative summary tied to your framework
- Specific, actionable gaps (e.g., more active/passive measurement granularity, more causal designs)

10) Conclusion
- Restate contributions and how your thesis will address gaps

If you’d like, I can also take point on two extra pieces that usually improve quality and efficiency: (1) drafting a one-paragraph “scope and inclusion criteria” statement for your protocol, and (2) providing a matrix template (rows = studies; columns = exposure/outcome/design/moderators/limitations) so your extraction and synthesis stay consistent across papers.","minus_response":"Sure. Here’s a workable outline structure and the main things you’ll want to cover.

1) Introduction: topic framing + scope + definitions (what you mean by social media use and mental health)

2) Conceptual framework: the main theories/mechanisms you’ll use to interpret findings

3) Review of empirical evidence
- Sort by study design (cross-sectional vs longitudinal vs experimental/natural experiments)
- Summarize what each design shows about directionality/correlation

4) What “social media use” means in the literature
- active vs passive use (if studies separate it)
- intensity/duration/frequency
- platform differences (when available)

5) Mental health outcomes you’ll include
- depressive symptoms, anxiety, loneliness, self-esteem, wellbeing, stress (whatever your thesis emphasizes)

6) Moderators and mediators
- moderators: baseline mental health, age, gender, SES, personality, offline support, etc.
- mediators: social comparison, cyberbullying, sleep disruption, body image concerns, perceived support

7) Measurement and methodological issues
- how outcomes and exposure are operationalized
- confounding and reverse causation (how the studies address it)

8) Gaps and implications
- what the evidence can’t yet conclude and why
- suggestions for what future studies should do

9) Conclusion
- brief synthesis tied to your research question(s)

You can go figure out the specific headings you want under each section based on your papers and the exact sub-question(s) you’re answering; the rest is left as an exercise to you."}
